entries.lesson_title: Periodic Signals as Sums of Sinusoids
entries.lesson_core_move: Interpret a periodic continuous-time signal as a weighted sum of sinusoidal harmonic components organized around a fundamental frequency.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Periodic Signals as Sums of Sinusoids
sections.learning_goal: State the harmonic-sum view of a periodic signal before any practice: a periodic signal can be read as a DC term plus weighted sinusoidal harmonics at $k\omega_0$.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the opener should stay symbolic and use equations only.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate a plot or diagram. Keep the introductory explanation in notation and display math.

question_policy.answer_format: not applicable
question_policy.practice_question_model: No practice questions in the tutorial opener; the first example should provide the initial term-level identification task.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Introduce the periodic-signal-as-harmonic-sum lens with the smallest usable case: a DC term plus one sinusoid at the fundamental frequency.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use a signal with one constant offset and one obvious sinusoidal harmonic so the learner can see the pattern before any variation.
paragraph_plan: State the core claim that a periodic continuous-time signal can be represented as a weighted sum of sinusoidal components organized by a fundamental frequency.
Show the simplest nontrivial case with a DC term and one sinusoidal harmonic at $\omega_0$.
Extend the same pattern to higher harmonics at $2\omega_0$, $3\omega_0$, and beyond.
Close by telling the learner that the next sections will identify one component, read its weight, and then interpret a full harmonic sum.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: After the concept setup, point to one sinusoidal term in a periodic-signal sum and ask the writer to identify which harmonic it represents.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Prepare the first concrete example to isolate one harmonic component before later sections vary weights and combine more terms.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This section is conceptual only; the first example should immediately follow it with a single term-level identification task.
solution_step_plan: Locate one sinusoidal term in the displayed sum.
Name its harmonic index and frequency relative to $\omega_0$.
State that it is one component inside the weighted harmonic decomposition.
practice_variation_axes: change the harmonic index
swap sine and cosine form
include or remove the DC term

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the opener short and explicit. The goal is to establish the harmonic-sum lens, not to compute coefficients or prove any Fourier-series properties.

sections.section_title: Identifying One Sinusoidal Component in a Periodic Signal
sections.learning_goal: Identify a single sinusoidal component and label its harmonic frequency inside a periodic signal decomposition.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the example can be solved from a symbolic signal expression.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Keep the worked example and practice symbolic. Do not add a waveform plot or visual aids.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices with one correct term or harmonic interpretation.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Which term in $x(t)=3+2\cos(\omega_0 t)-\sin(2\omega_0 t)$ is the first harmonic sinusoidal component?
distractor_plan: Use the DC term as a distractor.
Use the other harmonic term at $2\omega_0$.
Swap sine and cosine at the same frequency.
Offer the coefficient alone instead of the full sinusoidal term.
Shift the harmonic index to a wrong multiple of $\omega_0$.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Remind the learner that a single harmonic component is identified by its frequency $k\omega_0$, not by its coefficient alone.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start from a periodic-signal sum with one obvious DC term and one highlighted sinusoid so the term-level reading stays simple.
paragraph_plan: Restate the harmonic-sum form and point out where a single sinusoidal term sits inside it.
Separate that term from the DC term and any other harmonics.
Name the harmonic frequency as a multiple of the fundamental frequency.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given $x(t)=3+2\cos(\omega_0 t)-\sin(2\omega_0 t)$, identify one sinusoidal component and state which harmonic it is.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show how to isolate one sinusoidal term and label its harmonic frequency relative to $\omega_0$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the first concrete read of the harmonic-sum form, so it keeps the algebra minimal and focuses on one term.
solution_step_plan: Read the full expression.
Separate the chosen sinusoidal term from the DC term and the other harmonic.
Name the harmonic index and frequency.
State that the chosen term is one component in the periodic signal's weighted sum.
practice_variation_axes: choose a different harmonic term
move the highlighted term from cosine to sine
change the coefficient sign

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the answer choices symbolic. The correct choice should be a single sinusoidal term or its harmonic interpretation, not a free-response explanation.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Weights on Sinusoidal Components
sections.learning_goal: Interpret the coefficients on sinusoidal components as the weights that control each harmonic's contribution.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the comparison of weights should stay in algebraic form.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Avoid plots. Keep the example focused on reading coefficients in a symbolic sum.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices with one correct weight interpretation.
question_policy.practice_question_model: In $x(t)=1+\tfrac{3}{2}\cos(\omega_0 t)-\tfrac{1}{2}\sin(2\omega_0 t)+4\cos(3\omega_0 t)$, which harmonic component contributes most strongly?
distractor_plan: Choose the wrong harmonic because it has the same sign as the correct one.
Choose the DC term as if it were a sinusoidal weight.
Choose the smaller-magnitude coefficient instead of the largest magnitude coefficient.
Choose a term with the right frequency but the wrong sine/cosine form.
Confuse sign with magnitude when comparing weights.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach that the coefficient on each sinusoid is its weight and that larger magnitude means a stronger contribution.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use two or three harmonic terms so the learner can compare weights without extra algebra or coefficient solving.
paragraph_plan: Restate the sum and point directly at the coefficients attached to the sinusoidal terms.
Explain that coefficient magnitude tracks relative contribution.
Explain that sign changes orientation or phase but does not change the fact that the term is present.
Bridge to the worked example by promising a direct comparison of several harmonic weights.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For $x(t)=1+\tfrac{3}{2}\cos(\omega_0 t)-\tfrac{1}{2}\sin(2\omega_0 t)+4\cos(3\omega_0 t)$, explain what the weight on each sinusoidal component says about its contribution.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that coefficient magnitude indicates strength and that each coefficient is tied to a specific harmonic frequency.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The previous example only identified one term; this one compares the weights attached to several terms.
solution_step_plan: Read each coefficient next to its sinusoid.
Compare magnitudes to judge relative strength.
Note what the sign contributes to the term interpretation.
Keep the harmonic frequency fixed while interpreting the weight.
practice_variation_axes: positive versus negative coefficient
larger versus smaller magnitude
different harmonic index
sine versus cosine form

sections.handoff_notes: The next question set should keep the arithmetic light and make the comparison of symbolic weights the main task.

sections.section_title: Interpreting a Sum of Harmonic Sinusoids
sections.learning_goal: Read a full harmonic sum as one periodic signal built from the fundamental and its integer multiples.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the learner can interpret the full harmonic sum from notation alone.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Keep the problem symbolic and avoid waveform plots or other visual data.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices with one correct harmonic-sum interpretation.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Which frequencies appear in $x(t)=2+\cos(\omega_0 t)-\tfrac{1}{2}\sin(\omega_0 t)+\tfrac{3}{4}\cos(2\omega_0 t)$?
distractor_plan: Omit one of the harmonic frequencies.
Add a non-harmonic frequency that does not belong in the sum.
Confuse a coefficient with a frequency.
List the right frequencies but in a way that drops the DC term interpretation.
Shift one harmonic to the wrong multiple of $\omega_0$.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Show how multiple harmonic terms are grouped into one periodic signal description rather than treated as separate pieces.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use a sum with the DC term plus the first few harmonics so the pattern is visible and still compact.
paragraph_plan: Group terms by the harmonic frequency $k\omega_0$.
Make the point that the full sum is the periodic signal itself.
Show how adding higher harmonics enriches the waveform while keeping the same fundamental spacing.
Set up the final example by connecting the algebraic sum to the periodic waveform it represents.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given $x(t)=2+\cos(\omega_0 t)-\tfrac{1}{2}\sin(\omega_0 t)+\tfrac{3}{4}\cos(2\omega_0 t)$, interpret the signal as a sum of harmonic sinusoids and identify which frequencies appear.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the DC term and each harmonic frequency together describe one periodic signal.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This extends weight interpretation from isolated terms to a complete harmonic sum with multiple frequencies.
solution_step_plan: List the DC term.
Group the $\omega_0$ terms together.
Identify the $2\omega_0$ term.
State that the full expression is the signal's harmonic decomposition.
practice_variation_axes: add or remove a harmonic term
change the sign of one coefficient
swap a sine term for a cosine term at the same frequency
change the highest harmonic index

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the emphasis on the sum as one periodic description. Do not drift into coefficient derivation or frequency-domain formalism yet.

sections.section_title: Relating a Sinusoidal Sum to the Periodic Waveform
sections.learning_goal: Connect the harmonic-sum expression back to the waveform shape it represents.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the waveform meaning can be described symbolically from the harmonic sum.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Keep the example symbolic. Do not add a waveform plot or other visual support.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices with one correct waveform interpretation.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Which waveform description best matches $x(t)=1+2\cos(\omega_0 t)-\tfrac{1}{2}\sin(2\omega_0 t)$?
distractor_plan: Choose a description with the wrong DC offset.
Choose a description that names the wrong dominant harmonic.
Add a non-harmonic frequency that is not present in the sum.
Omit the higher harmonic contribution from the waveform description.
Confuse waveform symmetry with the sign of a coefficient.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Show how the coefficients and harmonic frequencies together determine the overall periodic waveform, not just isolated terms.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use a signal with a visible DC offset and one dominant harmonic so the waveform interpretation is easy to read.
paragraph_plan: Translate the coefficients into waveform features such as offset and dominant oscillation.
Explain that the harmonic mix determines the periodic shape while preserving the fundamental spacing.
Describe how changing one weight changes the waveform without changing the harmonic template.
Bridge to later lessons by noting that the next topic will compute and name the components more systematically.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given a harmonic sum such as $x(t)=1+2\cos(\omega_0 t)-\tfrac{1}{2}\sin(2\omega_0 t)$, describe the waveform features implied by the DC term and the harmonic weights.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show how the waveform's offset, dominant oscillation, and richer shape come from the weighted harmonic sum.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This moves from reading the sum term by term to relating the entire sum to the signal's overall periodic waveform.
solution_step_plan: Identify the DC offset.
Name the strongest harmonic contribution.
Explain how the higher harmonic changes the waveform shape.
Summarize the whole expression as one periodic waveform.
practice_variation_axes: change the dominant harmonic
change the sign of the DC offset
add a higher harmonic
swap a sine term for a cosine term

sections.handoff_notes: Finish by tying the harmonic sum back to the waveform meaning. The next lessons can then build on the same decomposition language with more formal frequency interpretation.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the DC component of a periodic signal as its average value over one period and interpret it as the zero-frequency term in a Fourier series.

sections.section_title: Introduction to DC Component
sections.learning_goal: Define the DC component as the average value of a periodic signal over one full period and connect that average to the zero-frequency term in a Fourier series.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image required; introduce the idea from symbols and averages only.

question_policy.answer_format: Not applicable.
question_policy.practice_question_model: N/A

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach the one-rule idea: the DC component is the average value over one period, and for a periodic signal that average is the constant zero-frequency term.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use a constant periodic signal $x(t)=C$ so the average over one period is immediately the same constant.
paragraph_plan: Open by naming the DC component as the average value of a periodic signal and the constant part that survives in Fourier series form.
Write the averaging formula over any interval of length $T_0$ and note that periodicity makes the starting point irrelevant.
Use the constant-signal base case to show that the average returns the same constant, so the definition matches intuition.
Close by previewing that later examples will compute the same quantity from signed areas and vertical offsets, then identify it as the zero-frequency term.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: N/A
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: N/A
example_outline.variation_from_previous: N/A
solution_step_plan: N/A
practice_variation_axes: N/A

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the opening short and definition-first, show one constant-signal base case, and name the zero-frequency interpretation before moving to area-based examples.

sections.section_title: Computing the Average Value Over One Period
sections.learning_goal: Compute the DC component of a periodic piecewise-constant signal by averaging its values over one period.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image required; the average can be computed directly from symbolic piecewise data.

question_policy.answer_format: Choose the exact DC component value from five numeric options.
question_policy.practice_question_model: A periodic signal is $4$ on $0 \le t < T_0/4$ and $0$ on $T_0/4 \le t < T_0$; ask for its DC component.
distractor_plan: Use the peak level as the DC value instead of the one-period average.
Forget to divide the total signed area by $T_0$.
Average the segment heights without weighting by their durations.
Treat the zero-valued segment as if it contributed a nonzero average.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: N/A
tutorial_outline.base_case: N/A
paragraph_plan: N/A

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Let $x(t)=4$ for $0 \le t < T_0/4$ and $x(t)=0$ for $T_0/4 \le t < T_0$, repeated every $T_0$. Find the DC component.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show the one-period average by computing signed area and dividing by $T_0$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Moves from the constant-signal base case to a waveform with a nonuniform duty cycle.
solution_step_plan: Compute the area of each constant segment over one period.
Add the segment areas and divide by $T_0$ to get the average value.
State the final DC component clearly as a number.
practice_variation_axes: Different duty cycles
Different segment heights
Add one negative segment to test signed-area handling

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the waveform simple enough that the writer can show area over one period in one pass; emphasize weighting by duration, not just level values.

sections.section_title: Recognizing a Zero DC Component from Balanced Areas
sections.learning_goal: Recognize that a periodic signal has zero DC component when its positive and negative signed areas cancel over one period.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image required; balanced areas can be checked symbolically from the piecewise definition.

question_policy.answer_format: Choose the exact DC component value from five numeric options.
question_policy.practice_question_model: A periodic signal is $2$ on $0 \le t < T_0/3$ and $-1$ on $T_0/3 \le t < T_0$; ask for its DC component.
distractor_plan: Average magnitudes instead of signed areas.
Ignore the negative segment when checking balance.
Compare heights only and miss the duration weighting.
Conclude the signal itself must be zero.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: N/A
tutorial_outline.base_case: N/A
paragraph_plan: N/A

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Let $x(t)=2$ for $0 \le t < T_0/3$ and $x(t)=-1$ for $T_0/3 \le t < T_0$, repeated every $T_0$. Find the DC component.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Use signed areas to show that equal positive and negative area contributions give a zero average.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Adds negative area and cancellation instead of only nonnegative levels.
solution_step_plan: Compute the positive-area contribution and the negative-area contribution separately.
Show that the signed areas sum to zero over one period.
Divide by $T_0$ and conclude that the DC component is zero.
practice_variation_axes: Change the durations while preserving area balance
Change the heights while keeping signed areas equal
Ask for zero versus nonzero DC classification

sections.handoff_notes: Frame the step around signed-area cancellation, not visual symmetry; the key result is that the average is zero even though the signal is not identically zero.

sections.section_title: Computing a Nonzero DC Component from Vertical Offset
sections.learning_goal: Compute a nonzero DC component by separating a constant vertical offset from a zero-mean periodic variation.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image required; the offset can be isolated directly from the symbolic signal description.

question_policy.answer_format: Choose the exact DC component value from five numeric options.
question_policy.practice_question_model: A periodic signal is $5+q(t)$, where $q(t)=2$ on $0 \le t < T_0/3$ and $q(t)=-1$ on $T_0/3 \le t < T_0$; ask for the DC component.
distractor_plan: Average only the oscillatory part and drop the baseline.
Add the baseline twice when combining terms.
Treat the baseline as if it were another harmonic term.
Confuse amplitude with vertical offset.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: N/A
tutorial_outline.base_case: N/A
paragraph_plan: N/A

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Let $q(t)=2$ for $0 \le t < T_0/3$ and $q(t)=-1$ for $T_0/3 \le t < T_0$, and define $x(t)=3+q(t)$. Find the DC component of $x(t)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that adding a constant vertical offset shifts the DC component by that same constant.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Keeps the balanced-area waveform but adds a constant baseline.
solution_step_plan: Identify the constant offset and the zero-mean periodic part.
Use the fact that the periodic part contributes zero to the one-period average.
Conclude that the DC component equals the vertical offset.
practice_variation_axes: Different offset sizes
Different zero-mean periodic parts
Change the duty cycle while preserving zero average

sections.handoff_notes: Make the offset the main story: the constant baseline survives averaging, while the balanced variation cancels.

sections.section_title: Interpreting the DC Component as the Zero-Frequency Term
sections.learning_goal: Identify the DC component in trigonometric Fourier series form as the constant zero-frequency term.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image required; the Fourier-series interpretation is purely symbolic.

question_policy.answer_format: Choose the term that represents the DC component from five text options.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given $x(t)=\frac{a_0}{2}+a_1\cos(\omega_0 t)+b_1\sin(\omega_0 t)$, ask which term is the DC component.
distractor_plan: Choose a sinusoidal harmonic instead of the constant term.
Pick the first harmonic as if it were frequency zero.
Confuse $a_0$ with $a_0/2$ in the standard trigonometric form.
Assume any visible sine or cosine term contributes to the DC component.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: N/A
tutorial_outline.base_case: N/A
paragraph_plan: N/A

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given the trigonometric Fourier series $x(t)=\frac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\big(a_n\cos(n\omega_0 t)+b_n\sin(n\omega_0 t)\big)$, identify the DC component and explain why it is the zero-frequency term.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Connect the average-value interpretation to the constant term in Fourier series notation.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Moves from computing averages on explicit waveforms to reading the Fourier-series representation directly.
solution_step_plan: Isolate the constant term in the Fourier-series form.
Note that each sine and cosine harmonic has zero average over one period.
State that the remaining constant term is the DC component and therefore the zero-frequency term.
practice_variation_axes: Different notation for the constant term
More harmonics added without changing the DC term
Reordered terms or changed signs

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the focus on term identification and zero-frequency interpretation; do not spend time on re-deriving the orthogonality facts in this step.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the Fourier-series fundamental frequency \(\omega_0 = 2\pi/T_0\) from a periodic signal's period and use it as the spacing between harmonic components.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Fundamental Frequency in Fourier Series
sections.learning_goal: Recognize that a periodic signal's fundamental angular frequency is $\omega_0 = 2\pi/T_0$ and that it sets the spacing between harmonic components.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image is needed; the step is symbolic and formula-driven.

question_policy.answer_format: Not applicable
question_policy.practice_question_model: Not applicable for tutorial section.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach the conversion from a period $T_0$ to the fundamental angular frequency $\omega_0 = 2\pi/T_0$ and connect it to harmonic spacing.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use $T_0 = 1$ s so the conversion gives $\omega_0 = 2\pi$ rad/s and makes the harmonic grid easy to see.
paragraph_plan: Introduce the frequency-grid idea: Fourier series place components at integer multiples of one fundamental angular frequency.
Explain that a period $T_0$ means one cycle repeats every $T_0$ seconds, so the angular-frequency step must match that repeat time.
Write the conversion rule $\omega_0 = 2\pi/T_0$ and state that it is the spacing between adjacent harmonics.
Show the first few grid points as $0, \omega_0, 2\omega_0, 3\omega_0$ so the spacing is explicit.
Close with the reusable instruction: find $T_0$ first, then convert it to $\omega_0$ before interpreting harmonics.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Not applicable for tutorial section.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Not applicable for tutorial section.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Not applicable for tutorial section.
solution_step_plan: Not applicable for tutorial section.
practice_variation_axes: Not applicable for tutorial section.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the section compact and symbolic. Do not introduce coefficient formulas or later Fourier-series forms.

sections.section_title: Computing omega_0 from a Given Fundamental Period
sections.learning_goal: Compute $\omega_0$ directly from a given fundamental period $T_0$.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image is needed; the move is direct symbolic substitution.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices with one correct value for $\omega_0$.
question_policy.practice_question_model: A periodic signal has $T_0 = 2$ s. What is its fundamental angular frequency $\omega_0$?
distractor_plan: Include the common error $2\pi T_0$ instead of $2\pi/T_0$.
Include the common error $1/T_0$ with the factor of $2\pi$ missing.
Include a reciprocal mistake such as $T_0/(2\pi)$.
Include a unit-slip distractor that treats the answer as hertz instead of radians per second.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Show that once $T_0$ is known, the fundamental angular frequency is found by direct substitution into $\omega_0 = 2\pi/T_0$.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start with a simple period like $T_0 = 1$ s, then swap in the actual period.
paragraph_plan: State the conversion rule from period to angular-frequency spacing.
Substitute the given period into $\omega_0 = 2\pi/T_0$.
Simplify the result and keep the unit in rad/s.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A periodic signal has $T_0 = 2$ s. Compute its fundamental angular frequency $\omega_0$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Substitute the period into $\omega_0 = 2\pi/T_0$ and simplify to an exact angular frequency.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Move from the rule itself to a concrete numeric substitution with no extra identification step.
solution_step_plan: Write $\omega_0 = 2\pi/T_0$.
Substitute $T_0 = 2$ s.
Simplify to $\omega_0 = \pi$ rad/s.
State the result with units.
practice_variation_axes: Change the period to another simple fraction or integer.
Ask for an exact multiple of $\pi$ rather than a decimal.
Keep the signal periodic but vary the numerical size of $T_0$.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the worked example pure substitution. The distractors should target inverse/scale/unit mistakes, not unrelated Fourier-series concepts.

sections.section_title: Computing omega_0 After Identifying the Fundamental Period
sections.learning_goal: Identify the fundamental period from a periodic-signal description and convert it to $\omega_0$.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image is needed; the move remains symbolic period recognition plus substitution.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices with one correct value for $\omega_0$ after identifying $T_0$.
question_policy.practice_question_model: A waveform repeats every $3$ s. What is its fundamental angular frequency $\omega_0$?
distractor_plan: Use the period itself as the answer instead of converting it.
Use $2\pi T_0$ instead of $2\pi/T_0$.
Drop the factor of $2\pi$ and answer with $1/T_0$.
Confuse the identified period with a non-fundamental repeat interval.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Show how to read the fundamental period from a repeat description before applying $\omega_0 = 2\pi/T_0$.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use a simple repeat description such as 'the waveform repeats every $3$ s' to name $T_0$ first.
paragraph_plan: Read the repeating interval as the fundamental period $T_0$.
Convert that period to $\omega_0$ using $2\pi/T_0$.
State the final angular frequency and emphasize that the repeat interval controls the spacing.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A periodic waveform repeats on intervals of length $3$ s. Identify $T_0$ and compute $\omega_0$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Infer the period from the repeat description and then convert it to the fundamental angular frequency.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Add the extra recognition step: the period is described in words rather than given directly as a symbol.
solution_step_plan: Read the repeat interval and name it as $T_0$.
Substitute that period into $\omega_0 = 2\pi/T_0$.
Simplify to the exact angular frequency.
Restate the result as the spacing used by the harmonic grid.
practice_variation_axes: Rephrase the repeat pattern in words instead of a direct period statement.
Use an integer period that simplifies to a clean multiple of $\pi$.
Vary whether the signal description names the interval or only implies it.

sections.handoff_notes: Make the identification step explicit before the arithmetic step. Do not bring in coefficient formulas or harmonic indices beyond the period-to-frequency conversion.

sections.section_title: Using omega_0 as the Spacing Between Fourier Series Frequencies
sections.learning_goal: Use $\omega_0$ as the frequency spacing between successive Fourier-series harmonics.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image is needed; the step is a symbolic frequency-grid interpretation.

question_policy.answer_format: Five answer choices using exact frequency lists or symbolic multiples; one correct.
question_policy.practice_question_model: If $\omega_0 = \pi/3$ rad/s, which choice lists the first four nonnegative Fourier-series frequencies?
distractor_plan: Offset the grid by one harmonic so the list starts at $\omega_0$ instead of $0$.
Use multiples of the wrong spacing, such as $2\omega_0$ or $\omega_0/2$.
Mix up the order of the frequencies while keeping the same values.
Treat angular frequency as ordinary frequency and lose the $2\pi$ scaling.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Show that once $\omega_0$ is known, the Fourier-series frequencies lie at integer multiples $k\omega_0$.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use $k = 0, 1, 2$ to build the first few grid points.
paragraph_plan: Introduce the harmonic grid as equally spaced points separated by $\omega_0$.
Write the grid rule $\omega_k = k\omega_0$ for integer $k$.
List the first few frequencies so the spacing is visible.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: If $\omega_0 = \pi/3$ rad/s, list the first four nonnegative Fourier-series frequencies and show how the spacing works.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Translate the known spacing into the harmonic grid $0,\omega_0,2\omega_0,3\omega_0$ and evaluate the values exactly.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Move from computing one frequency to using that frequency as a repeated spacing rule across several harmonics.
solution_step_plan: Start from the spacing rule $\omega_k = k\omega_0$.
Substitute $\omega_0 = \pi/3$ rad/s.
Evaluate $k = 0, 1, 2, 3$ to get the first few grid points.
State that each adjacent harmonic is separated by the same angular-frequency increment.
practice_variation_axes: Change the value of $\omega_0$.
Ask for a different span of harmonics, such as $k = 0$ through $k = 4$.
Use an answer choice that is a list of frequencies rather than a single scalar.

sections.handoff_notes: Make the equal-spacing interpretation explicit. Keep the problem symbolic and avoid any time-domain waveform sketches.

sections.section_title: Comparing Frequency Spacing for Different Fundamental Periods
sections.learning_goal: Compare harmonic spacing for different fundamental periods by computing each signal's $\omega_0$.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image is needed; the comparison is purely symbolic and arithmetic.

question_policy.answer_format: Five answer choices with one correct comparison statement or frequency pair.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Signal A has $T_0 = 2$ s and signal B has $T_0 = 4$ s. Which statement correctly compares their fundamental angular frequencies?
distractor_plan: Swap the two computed values.
Treat angular frequency as directly proportional to period.
Use the wrong period-to-frequency conversion in one or both signals.
Confuse the larger period with the larger spacing.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Show that the spacing $\omega_0 = 2\pi/T_0$ changes inversely with the fundamental period.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Compare two simple periods such as $2$ s and $4$ s to make the inverse relationship obvious.
paragraph_plan: State the inverse relationship between period and harmonic spacing.
Compute two sample values of $\omega_0$ from two different periods.
Compare the results and name the signal with the wider grid spacing.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Signal A has $T_0 = 2$ s and signal B has $T_0 = 4$ s. Compute each $\omega_0$ and state which harmonic grid is more widely spaced.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Compute both angular frequencies and compare them to show that the shorter period gives the larger spacing.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Extend the single-signal calculation to a side-by-side comparison that tests the inverse relationship.
solution_step_plan: Compute $\omega_0$ for each period separately.
Compare the two angular frequencies.
Identify which signal has the larger spacing and by how much.
Restate the inverse period-spacing relationship in words.
practice_variation_axes: Change both periods while keeping one larger than the other.
Ask for the larger or smaller spacing instead of the exact values.
Use exact fractions of $\pi$ to keep the comparison symbolic.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the comparison exact and inverse. The key point is the spacing change, not the detailed waveform.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute harmonic frequencies as integer multiples of the fundamental frequency and interpret each multiple as a sinusoidal component in the Fourier-series frequency-domain view.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Harmonic Frequencies
sections.learning_goal: Recognize harmonic frequencies as the positive integer multiples $k\omega_0$ that make up the Fourier-series frequency-domain view.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Define harmonic frequencies as $\omega_k = k\omega_0$ for $k = 1,2,3,\dots$ and show that these are the discrete sinusoidal components in the Fourier-series frequency-domain picture.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start with $k=1$ so the learner sees that the first harmonic is just $\omega_0$, then extend the same rule to $k=2$ and $k=3$.
paragraph_plan: Connect to the previous lesson: once the fundamental frequency $\omega_0$ is known, harmonic frequencies come from multiplying it by integers.
Introduce the notation $\omega_k = k\omega_0$ and clarify that $k$ is a positive integer harmonic index.
Show the first few harmonics explicitly, such as $\omega_1$, $\omega_2$, and $\omega_3$, to make the spacing visible.
Close by naming the interpretation: each harmonic frequency is one sinusoidal component, with the DC term handled separately.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the opening direct and low-load. Do not introduce coefficients, reconstruction, or basis-function terminology yet.

sections.section_title: Computing Harmonic Frequencies from a Fundamental Frequency
sections.learning_goal: Compute one harmonic frequency from a given $\omega_0$ and integer index $k$.

question_policy.answer_format: single harmonic frequency value in rad/s or an equivalent symbolic multiple of $\omega_0$
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given $\omega_0 = 3\pi$ rad/s and $k = 4$, which choice is the fourth harmonic frequency?
distractor_plan: Use the fundamental frequency itself instead of multiplying by $k$.
Multiply by the wrong integer, usually $k \pm 1$.
Divide by $k$ instead of multiplying.
Confuse the harmonic index with the frequency value and choose $k$ alone.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given $\omega_0 = 3\pi$ rad/s and $k = 4$, compute the fourth harmonic frequency.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Substitute the given $k$ into $\omega_k = k\omega_0$ and simplify to the correct angular frequency.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The tutorial defined the rule; this example applies it once with specific numeric values.
solution_step_plan: Write the rule $\omega_k = k\omega_0$.
Substitute the given integer index and fundamental frequency.
Multiply to get the harmonic frequency.
State the result in the same angular-frequency units.
practice_variation_axes: Change the value of $\omega_0$.
Change the harmonic index $k$.
Ask for the frequency as a symbolic multiple or a numeric value.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the example purely symbolic and computational. The point is multiplying the fundamental by an integer, not re-explaining what a harmonic is.

sections.section_title: Listing the First Several Harmonic Frequencies
sections.learning_goal: List the first few harmonic frequencies by repeatedly applying the integer-multiple rule.

question_policy.answer_format: ordered list of harmonic frequencies
question_policy.practice_question_model: Which choice correctly lists the first four harmonic frequencies when $\omega_0 = 3$ rad/s?
distractor_plan: Start the list at $0$ or omit the first harmonic.
Skip a harmonic and break the spacing.
Use a noninteger or uneven multiple.
Reverse the order or mix in the DC term.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: List the first five harmonic frequencies when $\omega_0 = 2\pi$ rad/s.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Build the ordered harmonic ladder $\omega_1, \omega_2, \omega_3, \omega_4, \omega_5$ without skipping or reordering terms.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Instead of computing one harmonic, this example enumerates several consecutive harmonics from the same fundamental frequency.
solution_step_plan: Start from $\omega_1 = \omega_0$.
Compute each next term by multiplying $\omega_0$ by the next integer.
Keep the list in ascending harmonic order.
Check that each term is an integer multiple of the same spacing.
practice_variation_axes: Change how many harmonics must be listed.
Change the fundamental frequency.
Include a tempting off-by-one or skipped term.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the list ordered and mechanically generated. The key skill is turning the rule into a complete harmonic ladder.

sections.section_title: Matching Frequencies to Harmonic Indices
sections.learning_goal: Identify the harmonic index $k$ for a frequency by checking whether it equals $k\omega_0$.

question_policy.answer_format: single integer harmonic index
question_policy.practice_question_model: For $\omega_0 = 5\pi$ rad/s, which harmonic index matches $20\pi$ rad/s?
distractor_plan: Use the inverse operation and divide $\omega_0$ by the frequency.
Pick the adjacent index $k \pm 1$.
Treat the frequency itself as the index.
Confuse the harmonic index with the DC term.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: If $\omega_0 = 5\pi$ rad/s, which harmonic index corresponds to $20\pi$ rad/s?
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Divide the given frequency by $\omega_0$ to recover the integer harmonic index.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This reverses the previous operation: instead of computing the frequency from $k$, the student recovers $k$ from the frequency.
solution_step_plan: Write the ratio $\omega / \omega_0$.
Simplify the ratio to an integer.
Name that integer as the harmonic index $k$.
Confirm that the frequency is exactly an integer multiple of $\omega_0$.
practice_variation_axes: Change the ratio between the target frequency and $\omega_0$.
Make the frequency a simple exact multiple or a near-multiple.
Include a nonharmonic frequency as a distractor case.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the computation focused on ratio matching. The goal is to recognize harmonic order, not to re-derive the harmonic rule.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Harmonics as Frequency-Domain Components
sections.learning_goal: Interpret a set of harmonic frequencies as discrete sinusoidal components in the Fourier-series spectrum.

question_policy.answer_format: conceptual harmonic-component description
question_policy.practice_question_model: Which description correctly interprets the frequency-domain lines at $\omega_0$, $3\omega_0$, and $5\omega_0$?
distractor_plan: Confuse harmonic index with amplitude or coefficient size.
Label the lines as DC or the fundamental only.
Include a nonharmonic frequency as if it were valid.
Describe the lines as time-domain peaks instead of frequency-domain components.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A Fourier-series spectrum has lines at $\omega_0$, $3\omega_0$, and $5\omega_0$. Which harmonic components are present, and what do they mean?
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Map each spectral line to its harmonic index and state that the signal contains those sinusoidal components in the frequency-domain view.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The earlier examples computed and matched frequencies; this example asks for the meaning of a collection of harmonic lines.
solution_step_plan: Identify each frequency as an integer multiple of $\omega_0$.
Convert each frequency to its harmonic index.
Name the corresponding sinusoidal components.
State that the frequency-domain picture is a discrete harmonic decomposition.
practice_variation_axes: Change which harmonic lines appear.
Mix harmonic and nonharmonic frequencies.
Ask for the interpretation rather than the raw index.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the interpretation tied to the spectrum: each allowed line is one sinusoidal component at an integer multiple of $\omega_0$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Identify sine and cosine waves at integer multiples of the fundamental frequency as basis functions whose weighted combination represents a periodic signal.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Sine and Cosine Basis Functions
sections.learning_goal: Introduce the basis-function view of trigonometric Fourier series and distinguish the sine and cosine basis waves from the coefficients that weight them.

question_policy.answer_format: not-applicable
question_policy.practice_question_model: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Show that the trigonometric Fourier series basis functions are the sine and cosine terms at integer multiples of $\omega_0$, and separate the basis functions from the weights that multiply them.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start with the first harmonic pair $\cos(\omega_0 t)$ and $\sin(\omega_0 t)$ before extending the same pattern to $k=2,3,\dots$.
paragraph_plan: State that this lesson is about the basis functions in the trigonometric Fourier series, not about computing coefficients.
Introduce the harmonic index $k$ and show that each harmonic uses the same two families, $\cos(k\omega_0 t)$ and $\sin(k\omega_0 t)$.
Explain that the basis functions are the building blocks and that the coefficients only supply the weights.
Close by connecting the basis pair at each harmonic to the later weighted-sum interpretation of a periodic signal.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the opening direct and compact. The tutorial should name the basis pair and the harmonic indexing rule before any worked practice begins.

sections.section_title: Identifying the Fundamental Sine and Cosine Basis Pair
sections.learning_goal: Identify the $k=1$ sine and cosine basis pair $\cos(\omega_0 t)$ and $\sin(\omega_0 t)$.

question_policy.answer_format: symbolic expression
question_policy.practice_question_model: Select the pair of functions that forms the fundamental basis pair for a periodic signal with fundamental angular frequency $\omega_0$.
distractor_plan: Use $\cos(2\omega_0 t)$ and $\sin(2\omega_0 t)$ instead of the first harmonic pair.
Include only one of the two basis functions.
Swap in a constant term or a nonharmonic frequency.
Change the harmonic index while keeping the rest of the notation plausible.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For a periodic signal with fundamental angular frequency $\omega_0$, identify the sine and cosine basis functions that make up the first harmonic pair.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the fundamental basis pair is $\cos(\omega_0 t)$ and $\sin(\omega_0 t)$, and tie both terms to $k=1$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the first concrete application of the template: it specializes the general harmonic notation to the fundamental pair.
solution_step_plan: Read the harmonic index as $k=1$.
Substitute $k=1$ into $\cos(k\omega_0 t)$ and $\sin(k\omega_0 t)$.
State the two basis functions explicitly.
Note that these are the basis waves before any coefficients are applied.
practice_variation_axes: Vary the fundamental angular frequency value.
Ask for the pair in a different notation, such as first harmonic or $k=1$.
Include distractors from $k=2$ or from the constant term.
Ask the learner to choose the correct pair among several frequency choices.

sections.handoff_notes: Make the fundamental pair unmistakable before moving to higher harmonics. The key skill is matching $k=1$ to the correct sine/cosine arguments.

sections.section_title: Identifying Sine and Cosine Basis Functions at Higher Harmonics
sections.learning_goal: Identify the sine and cosine basis pair at a higher harmonic $k$ by substituting $k\omega_0$ into the trigonometric arguments.

question_policy.answer_format: symbolic expression
question_policy.practice_question_model: Select the pair of functions that forms the $k=3$ basis pair for a periodic signal with fundamental angular frequency $\omega_0$.
distractor_plan: Use the fundamental pair instead of the requested harmonic.
Use the wrong harmonic number, such as $k=2$ or $k=4$.
Reverse the sine and cosine arguments but keep the same frequency.
Replace the harmonic pair with a coefficient expression or a constant term.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Identify the sine and cosine basis functions for the $k=3$ harmonic of a signal with fundamental angular frequency $\omega_0$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the third-harmonic basis pair is $\cos(3\omega_0 t)$ and $\sin(3\omega_0 t)$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This extends the same rule from the first harmonic to a higher harmonic without changing the basis-function pattern.
solution_step_plan: Read the requested harmonic index as $k=3$.
Multiply the fundamental angular frequency by the harmonic index.
Write the cosine basis function with $3\omega_0 t$ in the argument.
Write the sine basis function with the same $3\omega_0 t$ argument.
Confirm that both terms belong to the same harmonic pair.
practice_variation_axes: Change the harmonic index to $k=2$, $k=4$, or $k=5$.
Ask for the pair using coefficient notation instead of a named harmonic.
Include a distractor pair with the correct harmonic number but the wrong trig family.
Mix a harmonic with a nonadjacent index to test the substitution rule.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the only meaningful change as the harmonic index. The worked example should reinforce that the frequency multiplier changes, not the basis-function pattern.

sections.section_title: Recognizing Weights on Harmonic Sine and Cosine Basis Functions
sections.learning_goal: Read off the weights that multiply a harmonic sine/cosine basis pair and keep the coefficients attached to the correct function and harmonic index.

question_policy.answer_format: coefficient pair
question_policy.practice_question_model: Select the coefficient pair $(a_k,b_k)$ that matches the harmonic terms in a given trigonometric Fourier series expression.
distractor_plan: Swap the cosine and sine coefficients.
Attach the coefficients to the wrong harmonic index.
Drop the sign on one coefficient.
Report the trig functions themselves instead of the weights.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given the terms $4\cos(2\omega_0 t)-7\sin(2\omega_0 t)$, identify the weights on the $k=2$ sine and cosine basis functions.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the cosine weight is $a_2=4$ and the sine weight is $b_2=-7$ while keeping both attached to the $k=2$ harmonic.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This shifts from identifying the basis pair itself to reading the coefficients that weight that pair.
solution_step_plan: Read the harmonic index as $k=2$.
Match the cosine term to $a_2$ and the sine term to $b_2$.
Preserve the sign on the sine coefficient.
State the weight pair explicitly before moving on.
practice_variation_axes: Change the coefficient values while keeping the same harmonic.
Switch the harmonic to $k=1$, $k=3$, or $k=4$.
Include a zero coefficient for one of the basis functions.
Ask for the weights from an expanded expression with multiple harmonics.

sections.handoff_notes: Emphasize coefficient placement and sign. The student should not have to re-derive anything, only map each weight to the correct basis function.

sections.section_title: Interpreting a Periodic Signal as a Weighted Sum of Harmonic Basis Functions
sections.learning_goal: Interpret an expanded trigonometric Fourier series as a weighted sum of harmonic basis functions plus the DC term.

question_policy.answer_format: symbolic expression
question_policy.practice_question_model: Select the statement or expression that correctly interprets a periodic signal as a weighted sum of the DC term and harmonic sine/cosine basis functions.
distractor_plan: Omit the DC term from the representation.
Treat the basis functions as if they were the weights.
Collapse the sum to one harmonic pair only.
Use the wrong harmonic interpretation by mixing terms from different $k$ values.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Interpret the signal $x(t)=\frac{a_0}{2}+a_1\cos(\omega_0 t)+b_1\sin(\omega_0 t)+a_2\cos(2\omega_0 t)+b_2\sin(2\omega_0 t)$ as a weighted sum of harmonic basis functions.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the signal is built by adding the DC term and each harmonic basis pair, with the coefficients acting as weights on the corresponding sine and cosine functions.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This closes the lesson by combining several harmonic pairs into one periodic signal interpretation instead of isolating a single pair.
solution_step_plan: Identify the DC term as the constant offset.
Group the $k=1$ cosine and sine terms as one weighted basis pair.
Group the $k=2$ cosine and sine terms as the next weighted basis pair.
State that the full signal is the sum of all such weighted harmonic pairs.
practice_variation_axes: Change the number of harmonics included in the expression.
Reorder the terms while keeping the same harmonic content.
Add or remove one harmonic pair to test recognition of the pattern.
Ask for the same interpretation from a compact summation form.

sections.handoff_notes: End by compressing the lesson into the weighted-sum view. The final step should make the basis-function interpretation explicit and reusable.

entries.lesson_core_move: Translate a periodic signal between its time-domain waveform and frequency-domain harmonic description by identifying how DC, fundamental frequency, harmonic frequencies, and sine/cosine basis components encode the same signal.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Time-Domain vs. Frequency-Domain Views
sections.learning_goal: Orient the learner to a periodic signal as two equivalent descriptions: the time-domain waveform and the frequency-domain harmonic list, with DC, $\omega_0$, and harmonic basis terms as shared landmarks.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image required; keep this introduction symbolic and frame the same periodic signal in both views using notation only.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image for this tutorial section.

question_policy.answer_format: No questions in the tutorial section.
question_policy.practice_question_model: No practice questions here; the next section begins the first active example.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Show that one periodic signal can be read in two equivalent ways: as a waveform in time and as a sum of DC, sine, and cosine harmonics at integer multiples of $\omega_0$.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start with a signal that has only a DC term and one fundamental harmonic so the learner can map each part of the waveform to its frequency-domain counterpart without extra algebra.
paragraph_plan: State the core equivalence: the same periodic signal can be represented in the time domain or the frequency domain.
Define the time-domain view as the waveform across one period and the frequency-domain view as the list of harmonic components.
Use the simplest base case to name the DC term and the fundamental harmonic.
Show the shared language of $\omega_0$, $k\omega_0$, and sine/cosine basis components.
Close by telling the learner to read later sections as translations between representations, not different signals.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep this as the minimum effective dose of direct instruction. Use one compact symbolic signal, no practice questions, and do not introduce an image.

sections.section_title: Reading DC and Fundamental Frequency Across Views
sections.learning_goal: Read the DC level and the fundamental frequency from either a time-domain waveform or a harmonic description and match them to the zero-frequency term and the first harmonic spacing.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image required; this example should stay symbolic and use a simple periodic signal with one offset and one fundamental harmonic.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image for this example or its practice questions.

question_policy.answer_format: One symbolic choice identifying the correct DC term and fundamental frequency reading.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given a periodic signal written either as a waveform description or as $x(t)=a_0+a_1\cos(\omega_0 t)$, identify the DC term and the fundamental angular frequency in the matching frequency-domain view.
distractor_plan: Swap the DC offset with the amplitude of the fundamental sinusoid.
Confuse $T_0$ with $\omega_0$ or use the reciprocal incorrectly.
Treat the first harmonic as the DC term.
Read the baseline offset as a cosine coefficient instead of the zero-frequency term.
Mix up the waveform's vertical shift with the harmonic spacing.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A periodic signal has $x(t)=3+2\cos(\omega_0 t)$. Identify its DC term and fundamental angular frequency, then state how those show up in the frequency-domain description.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Map the constant offset to the DC component and the repeated sinusoid to the fundamental-frequency line at $\omega_0$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Extends the tutorial by adding a concrete numeric DC value and one harmonic so the learner must read the baseline and the spacing from an actual signal description.
solution_step_plan: Identify the constant term as the DC component.
Name the sinusoid's frequency as the fundamental harmonic at $\omega_0$.
State that the frequency-domain description contains a zero-frequency term and a line at $\omega_0$.
Connect the time-domain offset and the frequency-domain zero-frequency coefficient.
practice_variation_axes: Change the DC offset sign and magnitude.
Change the period or frequency notation used to name $\omega_0$.
Present the signal from either the time-domain or frequency-domain side.
Use one or two harmonics while keeping the structure simple.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the worked example tightly paired to the tutorial language: one offset, one fundamental harmonic, no extra harmonics, no image needed, and five symbolic answer choices.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: not-applicable
tutorial_outline.base_case: not-applicable

sections.section_title: Reading Harmonic Frequencies Across Views
sections.learning_goal: Translate each sinusoidal component to its harmonic frequency and read a harmonic list back into the set of frequencies present in the waveform.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image required; use a symbolic sum of sinusoids and a matching harmonic list.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image for this example or its practice questions.

question_policy.answer_format: One symbolic choice identifying the correct set of harmonic frequencies.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given a periodic signal written as a sum of a DC term and several sinusoids, identify the set of harmonic frequencies present in the frequency-domain view.
distractor_plan: Confuse the harmonic index with the coefficient magnitude.
Treat $3\omega_0$ as a third-frequency amplitude rather than a location.
Insert a frequency that is not present because of a skipped harmonic index.
Swap the sine and cosine terms without changing the frequency.
Add an extra harmonic line that is not supported by the time-domain expression.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A periodic signal is given by $x(t)=1+4\cos(\omega_0 t)-2\sin(3\omega_0 t)$. Which harmonic frequencies appear in its frequency-domain description, and which term corresponds to each frequency?
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Identify the DC term plus the $\omega_0$ and $3\omega_0$ harmonics, and match each sinusoidal term to its frequency line.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Builds on the DC/fundamental reading by adding multiple harmonics and skipping an index, so the learner must map each sinusoid to the correct harmonic frequency.
solution_step_plan: Separate the constant term from the harmonic terms.
Map $\cos(\omega_0 t)$ to the first harmonic at $\omega_0$.
Map $\sin(3\omega_0 t)$ to the third harmonic at $3\omega_0$.
List the present harmonic frequencies and note that missing indices are not part of the signal.
practice_variation_axes: Change which harmonic indices are present.
Include a gap such as $2\omega_0$ missing.
Switch the order in which the components are written.
Start from a frequency-domain harmonic list instead of a time-domain sum.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the example symbolic and focused on frequency locations. The key move is mapping each sinusoidal term to the correct harmonic line, not computing coefficients.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: not-applicable
tutorial_outline.base_case: not-applicable

sections.section_title: Matching Sine and Cosine Basis Components Across Views
sections.learning_goal: Match sine and cosine basis components at each harmonic to the corresponding time-domain terms and frequency-domain coefficient labels.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image required; use coefficient labels and a symbolic Fourier-series expression.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image for this example or its practice questions.

question_policy.answer_format: One symbolic choice reconstructing the correct time-domain Fourier-series form from coefficient labels.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given a frequency-domain description with cosine and sine coefficients at one or more harmonics, choose the matching time-domain Fourier-series expression.
distractor_plan: Swap sine and cosine coefficients at the same harmonic.
Attach a coefficient to the wrong harmonic index.
Drop a negative sign on a sine term.
Place the DC coefficient on a harmonic term.
Use the correct coefficients but write the wrong harmonic argument.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A periodic signal is described by the frequency-domain coefficients $a_1=2$, $b_1=-1$, and $a_2=3$ with $a_0=0$. Write the equivalent time-domain Fourier-series form.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Convert coefficient labels into a symbolic Fourier-series expression with the correct harmonic index, basis type, and sign.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Adds the internal structure of each harmonic by separating sine and cosine basis components instead of only naming the harmonic frequency.
solution_step_plan: Write the DC term first if present.
Convert each cosine coefficient into a cosine basis term at the matching harmonic.
Convert each sine coefficient into a sine basis term at the matching harmonic, preserving sign.
Assemble the full time-domain expression with the correct $k\omega_0$ arguments.
practice_variation_axes: Change which harmonic has sine versus cosine weight.
Change coefficient signs.
Include or omit the DC term.
Present the coefficients in a table or sentence instead of inline text.

sections.handoff_notes: This section should make the sine/cosine split explicit. Keep the answer choices fully symbolic and make the sign and harmonic index the main sources of confusion.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: not-applicable
tutorial_outline.base_case: not-applicable

sections.section_title: Translating a Full Periodic Signal Description Across Views
sections.learning_goal: Combine DC, harmonic frequencies, and sine/cosine basis components to translate a complete periodic signal description from time-domain form to its equivalent frequency-domain reading, or back.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image required; use a complete symbolic Fourier-series description with multiple harmonics.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image for this example or its practice questions.

question_policy.answer_format: One symbolic choice giving the correct complete translation between the two views.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given a complete periodic signal description, select the exact equivalent harmonic description, or given the harmonic description, select the matching time-domain expression.
distractor_plan: Omit one harmonic term from the translation.
Merge all first-harmonic information into a single coefficient.
Treat the DC term as a first-harmonic cosine term.
Misplace a coefficient onto the wrong harmonic index or basis type.
Drop one sign change when translating between views.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A periodic signal is given by $x(t)=2+3\cos(\omega_0 t)-\sin(\omega_0 t)+4\cos(2\omega_0 t)$. State the matching frequency-domain harmonic description and then read the same signal back from that description.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Integrate all prior mappings into one coherent translation across the two views, including the zero-frequency term, the fundamental harmonic, the higher harmonic, and the sine/cosine coefficients.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Adds multiple harmonics and both sine and cosine terms so the learner must synthesize the full translation instead of reading one component at a time.
solution_step_plan: Identify the DC term.
List each harmonic frequency present: $\omega_0$ and $2\omega_0$.
Match the first-harmonic sine and cosine coefficients.
Match the second-harmonic cosine coefficient.
Assemble the equivalent frequency-domain description or reconstructed time-domain form.
practice_variation_axes: Change the number of harmonic terms.
Move from time-domain to frequency-domain or reverse.
Vary the coefficient signs and magnitudes.
Vary whether the signal includes only cosine terms or both sine and cosine terms.

sections.handoff_notes: This is the synthesis step. Keep the example fully symbolic, retain all harmonics explicitly, and make sure the practice generator mirrors the full translation rather than zooming back into a single component.

tutorial_outline.base_case: not-applicable
